newsitem.title: GERMANY: Oil prices fail to ignite German inflation fears.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices fail to ignite German inflation fears.

text.p: Surging world energy prices have not yet ignited fears at the Bundesbank and in financial markets that inflation in Germany, Europe's largest oil importer, could soon wake from its slumber.
Inflation has so far remained "very relaxed" despite higher prices for crude oil and refined products, the Bundesbank said on Thursday.
"The price environment in Germany remains up to now very relaxed," the central bank said in its October report, noting that import prices fell in August despite higher energy prices.

Some economists believe that the gains in oil prices to their highest level since the 1990-91 Gulf crisis will not have a near-term impact on inflation because sharp price falls in other areas of the economy have offset fuel prices.
"The higher energy prices for now will not have much effect," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS in Frankfurt.

Fahrinkrug said a softening of the mark against the dollar and rising crude oil prices -- up around 40 percent in the last four months to about $25 per barrel -- have sparked worries about mounting import price pressures.

"There have been periods when the Bundesbank was concerned about such trends," Fahrinkrug said. "However, at the moment it seems to be relaxed about oil prices and statements suggest that it would even prefer to see a slightly stronger dollar."

Higher energy prices were already reflected in provisional consumer price data from German states for September, with heating oil prices rising 11.7 percent in North Rhine-Westphalia on a monthly basis and 22.3 percent on a year-on-year basis.
But the increase did not prevent the state's cost of living falling 0.1 percent for the month, as it did in other states.
Indeed, some economists said the direct impact of rising crude prices was often overestimated in Germany.

"For the time being, inflation fears are not showing up," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs. "We still have stable influences from other traded goods prices, such as food and textiles, to make it benign."

But he said that when help from other sectors came to an end -- and if oil prices remained buoyant -- a 10 percent increase in the price of crude oil in marks would boost consumer prices by about a tenth of a percentage point.

"It's not insignificant but the environment is so favourable that it has been neutralised," Mayer said of the increase in oil prices, which has been linked to strong demand, low heating oil stocks and tensions in the Middle East.
Some economists, however, believe current energy prices, if sustained, could fuel modest growth in inflation in Germany as the higher prices filter through.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a recent report that the "bullish oil price scenario obviously has negative implications for the future path of inflation across the major economies".
It said France and the United States would run the biggest risk of higher inflation, while Germany could also suffer.
But UBS's Fahrinkrug said the German economy was not strong enough for companies to pass on price increases right now.
"You would have inflation fears if demand was strong enough for companies to pass on cost increases but they cannot. That's the benefit right now," Fahrinkrug said.
But Mathias Haffner at BZW said the impact from higher oil prices could begin showing up soon in data.
"I expect to see some effect, especially in October. We will no longer see negative numbers in consumer prices on a month-on-month basis," Haffner said.
He said heating oil suppliers would keep ratcheting up prices during the autumn as demand rises but that the impact on the economy so far had not yet caused alarm.
"Germany has digested the higher prices so far rather well, so I don't think it will be much of a concern to the Bundesbank," Haffner added.
